SPORTS | Concussion

By: Liz Fish | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
What are the long-term impacts of repetitive head injury in contact sports, and what is being done about it, what are the latest scientific findings. With the build up to World Cup Rigby what is being

Unique Selling Point:
28 years old Australia rugby player Heather Anderson’s brain autopsy results released in early July shocked the rugby world, she had severe CTE, Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy. She retired from rugby because of a shoulder injury and committed suicide a year later, she did not know she had CTE, highlighting once again the danger of repetitive head injury in contact sports. CTE is a serious brain disease caused by repetitive concussion and is only detected after death. It’s very distinctive from other brain degeneration and entirely caused by repetitive head injury/concussion. Over the last few years there have been several law suits in which retired players have sued their sporting bodies for damagers and inadequate protection. With World Cup Rugby on the horizon what is SA rugby doing to protect their players and the game?

Summary:
Pat Lambie retired from rugby 4 years ago because of 3 significant concussions, his neurologists advised him to get out of the game. But for a year and half after retiring he continued to suffer from severe headaches and depression. Lambie is open about the problems of suffering from concussion and the extraordinary pressures on players, which leads to further anxiety and depression making recovery even more difficult. He has valuable insights to share on retiring from rugby due to concussion and the fears of long term brain disease.

Further information:
Prof Jon Patricios is one of the world experts and co- authored the Consensus on Concussion report which looked at over 14000 papers on concussion and will speak to the latest scientific conclusions, treatment and diagnosis of this extremely complex condition. Concussion relies on the player/patient to describe their symptoms and often they are unable to accurately reflect their state of health and so as part of the independent diagnosis SA Rugby have been running saliva tests on their players which have significant biomarkers post concussion or sub concussive events. The are also running studies with instrumental mouth guards with accelerometers in them measuring the force that players have endured to assist early detection. South Africa concussion programs of diagnoses and prevention are world class and discussed globally. Clint Readhead chief medical officer and registered physiotherapist will speak about what changes are being made in the game to protect the players and the game.

Extra Budget Items:
Liz will have to fly to Durban, then JHB and then return to Cape Town. The presenter will have to fly to Durban return flight to JHB.

Opening sequence in the forest on the bridge
Script: It took 18 months - for Springbok Pat Lambie to come to terms with his decision to retire from rugby, struggling with deep depression - and a battered body.
He was one of the brightest and most versatile talents in South Africa rugby - playing 56 Tests in his 10-year career
Upsound Commentary: Here we go, Pat Lambie… to give the Sharks a lead once more.
Script: Nicknamed the “baby-faced assassin”, he started out at 18 with the Sharks, was named man of the Match in the 2010 Currie Cup final, and by 21 he was playing for South Africa.
Commentary: Under the most intense pressure Patrick Lambie nails it! Well he’s only a little fella Patrick Lambie, but he’s got nerves of steel.
Script: A crippling knee injury, while playing for the French team Racing 92, grounded Lambie… but this blow two years earlier , was the beginning of the end
Upsound Stander hit (fade to black)
LINK A series of major concussions forced Pat Lambie into early retirement at the peak of his career, he was just 28 at the time, it’s now 4 years later and he is still the most prominent South African rugby player to speak out about this
Pat 38 00:07:03:27 the rugby environment is very much. Who's the bravest, you know? Who's the. Strongest…..…. so tricky to walk into the room with it's huge specimens of human beings…….. Very macho and to be like, Sorry, I got a sore head. 00:07:36:28 Much easier to walk into a room if you're on crutches………… you should be feeling better by now because it's been weeks or it's been months. …..it's not an easy conversation to keep having over and over again with your coach, with your doctor, with your teammates.
Script: At the time of his retirement he suffered crippling headaches and burning eyes - taking longer and longer to recover from blows. Doctors feared long-term damage.
PAT 37 00:03:37:Govan: How have you been since then
Pat 37 00:03:43:13 the first 18 months was extremely difficult and I was still suffering from some symptoms. 00:04:15:07 They were more related to depression. …. I was getting very anxious and nervous about things, obviously in the back of my mind and wondering whether I was going to be okay in the long term, whether I was going to ever feel normal again. …….
Script: But in July, a test match building up to this year’s World Cup - thrust concussion back into the spotlight.
Commentary:
Script: Scrumhalf, Grant Williams, was knocked unconscious; Eerily familiar for Lambie
Pat “seeing him being knocked out cold and whiplash onto the ground and then stretcher and all of that was. Yeah. Shivers down the spine. I think for everyone watching
Script: Williams was stretchered off the field, but recovered in time to be named in the World Cup squad.
LINK: There is a concussion in nearly every professional rugby game. So the big question is how many knocks does it take before a player suffers long term brain damage
Jon: So the honest answer to that is we don't know. Having said that, it's still important that the game acknowledges that there may be a cumulative effect to these head injuries.
Script: Prof Jon Patricios speaks for the INTERNATIONAL CONSENSUS GROUP ON CONCUSSION - which informs much of the changes seen in collision sport.
Govan: what is the research showing us about concussions? What do we understand now?
Jon “Conditions such as depression, anxiety and suicide risk, there does not seem to be an increased risk of people that play contact and collision sport, and that applies to both amateur and professionals
Script: But the jury is still out on the growing body of evidence of long-term brain damage at a professional level, with extreme positions held on both ends of the debate, causing major unease in the game's corridors of power.
The latest case - 28-year-old Australian player Heather Anderson: -diagnosed after death with the brain disease Chronic traumatic encepha-lo-pathy - or CTE after her suicide - last year.
This despite her mother insisting she wear headgear - since starting to play rugby at the age of 5k - but the science shows that the cap only protects the skull…not the brain knocking around inside
Illustration head blow without concussion
In Britain more than 200 former amateur and professional players… are suing their unions for negligence and failure to protect them from brain injuries. One of them … is 2003 World Cup winner, England’s Steve Thompson, ….diagnosed with early onset dementia. Others claim they have suffered permanent neurological injuries including Parkinsons, Alzheimer’s and especially CTE.
Govan: Are you still concerned about that?
Pat I cling on to, an opinion of one of the doctors who, ah, I saw in the a small percentage of people who deal with head trauma extremely well. Most of us deal with it fine, and you get a small percentage of people who deal with it really badly.
It's almost like the card that you are dealt. …..…. I don't want to spend my days feeling anxious and worried about what may or may not come in my in my old age.
Upsound of kids playing
Script: Because there is no visible injury, concussion can be complex to detect,… especially the sub concussive or minor blows - which present the bigger problem
LINK: Successful concussion treatment relies on the players being honest with themselves, their coaches and their doctors, what rugby needs is an independent test.
Script: And they’re getting there: …..after six years of studying players’ saliva, they can now diagnose concussion …..from changes in the make-up of the saliva. Kyle Peyper, sports scientist at Lions Rugby, is part of two major international studies.
Kyle “We collect a sample at the beginning of the season and then after every game
Script: And most promising ….is that they have also found a recovery signature in the saliva - removing any lingering doubts from the player’s mind ….as to whether or not they have made a complete recovery.
Pat: 00:13:38:23 it would be game changing if the decision to return to play was taken away from player. Team doctor. Team coach.
Script: That's a scenario becoming increasingly possible….. as technology is deployed to answer important questions. Like,… at what gravitational force does a blow cause concussion? It's something being measured with smart mouth guards.
Kyle The chip is in the front and they have all their accelerometers and all their monitors are in the front.
Script: After each game …the data is downloaded
00.23 These graphs are the G force that each impact has given as you will see this player had a red flag for this session which is there and that gives us the Gforce which is 52 G force and the location
Script: Currently they don’t know at what G force concussion occurs…., but by measuring both big and small hits ….the player and the medical team have a lot more to work with
Jon: 00:02:22:23 - What worries us more is where concussions are not identified. The player plays on and places himself or herself at greater risk
Upsound
A Super Rugby match Pat Lambie played in 2012 ….is a perfect example
Pat 39 00:00:23:25 I had a head knock, I think it was in the 20 odd minutes into the game, um, and carried on playing and finished the first half …….…. I had kicked penalties …. was catching and passing was carrying on. But I only came round when I was in the change room the half time talk, and I just started crying because I actually didn't know how I got there, what the score was, what I'd done on the field beforehand.
Govan And you can’t remember any of that?
PAT: No, my memory of it is footage.
Upsound from game
Script: And if the first concussion is missed, a second blow soon after can be fatal.
But SA Rugby Union chief medical officer Clint Readhead says the good news is that the immediate head risk assessment has brought down missed concussions from 56% to 13%
Govan 00:20:17:04 -There's been a greater awareness around concussions in rugby over the last few years, ….more people hesitating to ……let their kids play….the game.
00:20:36:23 Clint: I think the CTE lawsuits have driven that.00:05:02:12 we want to do as much as we can to mitigate concussion in the sport. I think it's important to state that we'll never get to a point where there is zero risk in the sport.00:22:03:27 but I will say the game is in a good space, it's never had so much attention to making it safer
Script: The culture in World Rugby has changed with strict enforcement of dangerous play regulations and lowering tackle heights. The urgency has driven scientific innovation and concussion is now considered a treatable condition. But ultimately it's a high impact, collision sport - primed athletes running at each other with enormous force
Pat 38 00:08:27:03 Pat: I'm hoping that it's becoming easier for players to acknowledge that concussion is a very, very serious injury and you have to treat it properly and you have to be fully recovered before you run onto the field again, and you're silly if you don't.
Upsound of family

South Africa concussion programs of diagnoses and prevention are world class and discussed globally. Clint Readhead chief medical officer and registered physiotherapist will speak about what changes are being made in the game to protect the players and the game.
